title: Product Name Research v3
summary: Third pass product naming with a completely new direction.
content:
Product Name Research v3: The "Lemonade Stand" Edition

Steffen | 2026-03-15 For Patrik. Third pass. New direction entirely.

What Patrik Said (The Brief)

"Names aren't there yet. I loved Loft."

Then he dropped two new directions:

  1. "Lemonade Stand" energy. Anyone can start a business. A kid or an adult. The image of a kid at a folding table with a pitcher, a sign, and a dream. Universal. Warm. Immediate. No one needs to explain what a lemonade stand is.

  2. "The Team." Literal. Clean. Direct. "Open The Team." "Check The Team." Your AI team. That's it.

And the product truths he wants the name to carry:

  • You can START a business from inside the game. Not just manage one.
  • A 16-year-old or a 55-year-old, doesn't matter.
  • "A million worlds, one platform."
  • "The fun way to run your business."
  • "Young people love it, old people can't live without it."

Why v1 and v2 Missed

v1 and v2 were smart. They followed the rules of tech naming perfectly. Invented words, foreign language roots, sharp phonetics, ownable trademarks.

But Patrik's reaction tells me something important: this product doesn't want to sound like a tech product. It wants to sound like a THING. A real, tangible, human thing. Loft worked because everyone knows what a loft is. You can picture it. You can feel the light coming through the windows. You can smell the wood floors.

"Kova" is a great tech name. But you can't picture a kova. You can't feel one. It lives in your head, not your gut.

The lemonade stand direction is the opposite of Kova. It's the most REAL thing you can name. Every person on Earth can picture a lemonade stand. That's the energy Patrik wants.

"The Team" is the same instinct from a different angle. It's not clever. It's not foreign. It's just... what it is. Your team. Plain English. Done.

The new rule: The name should be something you could point to in real life.

Part 1: Dissecting "Lemonade Stand" Energy

What makes "lemonade stand" resonate isn't the words. It's the FEELING:

  • Anyone can do it. No credentials needed. No MBA. No funding round. Just you and an idea.
  • It's the first business. The universal starting point. Before Stripe, before Shopify, before LLCs and quarterly taxes, there was a kid with a sign.
  • It's fun. Nobody dreads running a lemonade stand. It's play that turns into profit.
  • It scales. Every billionaire's "started from nothing" story is a lemonade stand story dressed up.
  • It's generational. Your grandma ran one. Your kid runs one. The concept hasn't changed in 100 years.
  • It's visual. You see it immediately. Table, pitcher, hand-written sign, summer day.

Names with this energy feel:

  • Familiar (real English words)
  • Warm (not clinical, not techy)
  • Approachable (no barrier to entry)
  • Slightly playful (without being childish)
  • Physical (you could touch it, build it, sit at it)

Part 2: Dissecting "The Team" Energy

"The Team" works differently:

  • Literal. It says exactly what it is. Your AI team.
  • Ownership. It's YOUR team. "My team is on it." "Check The Team." "The Team handled it."
  • Confidence. Having a team is a power move. A solo business owner who says "I've got a team" feels upgraded.
  • Universal language. Every human knows what a team is. Every language has a word for it.
  • It answers the question. "How do you get all that done?" "I've got The Team."

The risk with "The Team" specifically:

  • "The" makes it clunky. "Open The Team" vs "Open Loft." Extra syllable, extra friction.
  • SEO nightmare. "The team" returns 10 billion results.
  • Can't become a verb. "I teamed that" doesn't work.
  • It's generic enough to feel like a feature name, not a product name.

But the VIBE is right. The name should make you feel like you have a team.

Part 3: The New Territory

v1 explored: real words repurposed, invented words, abstract concepts, gaming references. v2 explored: Italian words, start-from-zero metaphors, verb potential. v3 explores: everyday objects and spaces that feel like starting something.

The naming territory is now:

Physical things a business owner touches, sees, or stands behind.

Not metaphors. Not foreign words. Not invented syllables. Real things from real life that carry the RIGHT associations.

Part 4: The Candidates

Tier 1: The "Lemonade Stand" Lane

Names that evoke starting something, building something, the first day of your business.

1. STAND

Your lemonade stand. Your hot dog stand. Your stand at the market. The first business structure humanity ever built: a person, standing behind their thing, selling to the world.

  • One syllable. Five letters. Clean.
  • "Open my Stand." "Check Stand." "I run everything from my Stand."
  • It's physical. You can picture it. A stand at a market. A stand at a fair. A kid's lemonade stand.
  • It carries the "start from zero" energy perfectly. A stand costs nothing to build.
  • It also means to STAND for something. To take a stand. To stand your ground. Double meaning.
  • A 16-year-old: "I built my first business on Stand." Cool.
  • A 55-year-old: "My operation runs through Stand." Confident.
  • "A million stands, one platform." Works.
  • "The fun way to run your Stand." Works.

Trademark check: Stand (standapp.com) exists as a Mac app for standing desk reminders. Very small, different category. "Stand" as a general word is hard to trademark broadly, which cuts both ways: harder for competitors to block you, but harder for you to own exclusively.

2. BENCH

Where work gets done. The workbench. The judges' bench. "From the bench" means from where decisions are made. In sports, the bench is where your team waits to be put in the game.

  • One syllable. Five letters.
  • "Open Bench." "Check Bench." "My Bench is running."
  • Your agents sit on the bench until you put them in. You manage from the bench.
  • Workbench energy: tools laid out, organized, productive.
  • It's tangible. Everyone has sat on a bench or worked at one.
  • The sports metaphor FITS: "Put Bobby in." "Check who's on the bench."

Trademark check: Bench Accounting (bench.co) is a major bookkeeping platform. $100M+ raised. SMB audience. Too close. DEAD.

3. POST

The trading post. The outpost. The command post. A post is where you plant your flag and run operations from. It's also where you POST updates, POST results, POST your work.

  • One syllable. Four letters.
  • "Open Post." "Check my Post." "I manage everything from Post."
  • Military command post energy without being aggressive.
  • Trading post energy: where business happens, where people come to trade.
  • "Post" as a verb: your agents post updates, post results. Built-in.
  • The frontier vibe: you're building an outpost in new territory.

Trademark check: The Washington Post. PostHog (analytics). Postman (API platform). Postiz (social media). Too much collision. DEAD.

4. SHOP

The simplest business word in English. "Open up shop." "Set up shop." Everyone's first instinct when they start a business.

  • One syllable. Four letters.
  • "Open Shop." "Check Shop." "My Shop is running."
  • "Set up Shop" IS the product pitch. You open the app and set up shop.
  • It's the adult version of the lemonade stand. The kid grows up and opens a shop.
  • A million shops, one platform. Direct.
  • Grandma gets it. Teenager gets it.

Trademark check: Shopify dominates this territory completely. "Shop" is their verb, their app, their entire brand identity. The Shop App by Shopify has 100M+ downloads. DEAD.

5. TABLE

The kitchen table where every business starts. The boardroom table. The negotiating table. "Come to the table." "Put it on the table." "A seat at the table."

  • Two syllables. Five letters.
  • "Open Table." "Check my Table." "I run it from my Table."
  • The kitchen table is THE universal small business origin. Every founder started at a table.
  • The boardroom table is the destination. Table carries you from start to scale.
  • "A seat at the table" = access, opportunity, being taken seriously.
  • "Bring it to the Table." "What's on the Table?"

Trademark check: OpenTable (restaurant reservations). Airtable (database platform). Timetable, Roundtable... the word "table" is heavily used in tech. Specifically, OpenTable owns "table" in app contexts. DEAD.

6. STOOP

The front stoop. Where neighbors gather. Where business ideas are born over conversation. Where you sit and watch the world go by. A New York City stoop. A porch. Community, accessibility, ground level.

  • One syllable. Five letters.
  • "Open Stoop." "Check Stoop." "I'm on the Stoop."
  • The stoop is the most democratic space in a city. Everyone is welcome.
  • "Stoop sale" = the original marketplace. The OG lemonade stand for city kids.
  • It's street-level. Ground floor. No barriers.
  • Patrik's East Coast DNA (DC, Silver Spring, Maryland) connects to stoop culture.

Trademark check: Stoops (social events app) existed briefly. Mostly clear. Unusual enough to be ownable.

Risk: Not everyone knows "stoop." Regional. Might not land in the Southwest or Midwest.

7. LOT

The parking lot where the pop-up shop sets up. The market lot. The lot where the food trucks park. "I got a lot." A piece of land. The most basic unit of business real estate.

  • One syllable. Three letters.
  • "Open Lot." "Check my Lot." "What's happening in my Lot?"
  • A lot is empty until you build on it. Start from zero = start with a lot.
  • "A million lots, one platform." Direct.
  • It's TINY. Three letters. Instant to type, say, remember.
  • "Got a lot going on" = double meaning. Your lot IS a lot.

Trademark check: Relatively clean in software/AI. "Lot" is so common it's hard to own but also hard for anyone to claim exclusively. ParkingLot (various). No major conflicts in the space.

Risk: Three letters might feel too thin for a product with this much ambition. "Lot" also means "a bunch of stuff" which dilutes the real-estate meaning.

Tier 2: The "Your Team" Lane

Names where the product IS your team. Literal, direct, confident.

8. CREW

Not "The Team." Just Crew. Your crew. The people (agents) who have your back. "I've got a crew." Crew is warmer than "team." A team is organized. A crew is loyal.

  • One syllable. Four letters.
  • "Open Crew." "Check Crew." "My Crew is on it."
  • "I've got a Crew" sounds like a power statement. Confident. Street. Real.
  • Construction crews. Film crews. Flight crews. People who get things DONE.
  • "Crew: The fun way to run your business." Natural.
  • "Build your Crew from scratch." That's the product.
  • A 16-year-old: "Check my Crew." Sounds like a video game. Perfect.
  • A 55-year-old: "I run everything through Crew." Sounds professional.

Trademark check: CrewAI exists (open-source AI agent framework). Direct competitor. Squarely in our space. This is a problem but not necessarily fatal: CrewAI is a developer framework, not a consumer product. The audiences are different. But "crew" in the AI agent space = CrewAI in most people's minds right now.

Risk: CrewAI association is real. Anyone searching "Crew AI" or "Crew agents" hits CrewAI first. Would need to outbrand them, which is doable but requires energy.

9. SQUAD

Your squad. The group that rolls with you. More casual than "team," more energy than "crew."

  • One syllable. Five letters.
  • "Open Squad." "Check Squad." "My Squad handled it."
  • Military origin (small tactical unit) gives it a "get things done" edge.
  • Gaming culture LOVES "squad." Squad up. Squad goals. Immediately understood.
  • "Build your Squad." "Join the Squad." "Squad up."
  • The word has generational crossover: millennials know it, Gen Z knows it, boomers know it.

Trademark check: Multiple Squad-branded companies (Squad social app, Squad robotics, etc.) but the Squad social app shut down. Relatively open in AI/business.

Risk: "Squad" might feel too casual for B2B. "I run my company through Squad" sounds informal. Could work FOR the brand (fun, accessible) or against it (not serious enough for enterprise).

10. LINEUP

Your lineup. Like a baseball lineup. Like a police lineup. Like a music festival lineup. "Check the lineup." "Who's in the lineup?" Your agents are your lineup, and you set the order.

  • Two syllables. Six letters.
  • "Open Lineup." "Check my Lineup." "The Lineup is stacked."
  • Sports energy: your agents are your starting lineup. You choose who plays.
  • Festival energy: exciting, curated, the best acts in one place.
  • "Build your Lineup" = build your team of agents.

Trademark check: Lineup (lineup.com) exists as a workforce management tool. Different product (scheduling/time tracking) but close enough in B2B SaaS to cause confusion. Risky.

Risk: Two syllables is fine but less punchy than one. The word is also very common in everyday English, which makes SEO hard.

11. ROSTER

Your roster. Who's on the team. Like checking the roster for a game.

  • Two syllables. Six letters.
  • "Open Roster." "Check the Roster." "My Roster is full."
  • Sports DNA: every team has a roster. You draft agents onto your roster.
  • "Build your Roster from scratch." Clean.
  • It implies both the PEOPLE and the ORGANIZATION. A roster is a list, but it represents a team.

Trademark check: Roster (getroster.com) is a talent booking platform. Different space but same "team management" concept. Some overlap. Manageable.

Risk: "Roster" is functional but not emotional. It describes WHAT the product tracks (your team) but not HOW it feels. It's a spreadsheet word, not a game word.

Tier 3: The Sweet Spot (Lemonade Stand Energy + Team Energy)

These are the ones that combine both directions: the warmth and accessibility of "anyone can start" with the confidence of "you've got a team."

12. CORNER

The corner store. The corner office. Your corner of the internet. "Hold down the corner." In business, "corner" means dominance: "corner the market." In neighborhoods, the corner is where everything happens.

  • Two syllables. Six letters.
  • "Open Corner." "Check my Corner." "I run it from my Corner."
  • "Hold down your Corner" = own your space. Run your business. Defend your territory.
  • The corner store is the lemonade stand that grew up. Kid sells lemonade on the corner, adult runs a business from the Corner.
  • "Corner the market" is built into the name. Ambition is baked in.
  • Street culture DNA. Patrik's DC background. The corner is where you grow up, where you hustle, where you build.
  • "A million corners, one platform." Everyone gets their own corner.

Trademark check: Cornerstone OnDemand (HR/LMS). Corner (corner.com doesn't exist as a product). The word "corner" is surprisingly clean in AI/SaaS. No major conflicts found.

Risk: "Corner" could feel small. "I run my operation from my Corner" works, but at scale, "Corner" might feel like a limitation. Counter: the corner store is the BACKBONE of every neighborhood. It's small but it's everything.

13. BLOCK

The block you grew up on. Building blocks. Blockchain (minus the chain). "Around the block." "New kid on the block." The block is your neighborhood, your territory, your world.

  • One syllable. Five letters.
  • "Open Block." "Check my Block." "I'm on the Block."
  • Building blocks = you build your business piece by piece. Lego energy.
  • "Run the block" = own your territory. Street energy meets business energy.
  • "New kid on the Block" = someone just starting out. Perfect for "start from zero."
  • The block is where everyone knows you. Community. Roots.
  • A 16-year-old building blocks. A 55-year-old running the block.

Trademark check: Block, Inc. (formerly Square, Jack Dorsey's company). $50B+ market cap. They OWN "Block" in fintech/business tools. DEAD.

14. YARD

The front yard. The backyard. The schoolyard. Where kids play. Where businesses start (yard sale, backyard BBQ turned catering company). "In my yard" = on my turf.

  • One syllable. Four letters.
  • "Open Yard." "Check my Yard." "What's happening in the Yard?"
  • "Yard sale" is the lemonade stand's cousin. Same energy: you put stuff out, people come.
  • Scotland Yard = command center. Harvard Yard = the center of everything.
  • Construction: the yard is where materials are stored, where work stages from.
  • "A million yards, one platform." Everyone gets their own yard to build in.

Trademark check: Yard (various small companies). No major conflicts in AI/SaaS. Relatively clean.

Risk: "Yard" has construction/industrial associations (lumber yard, junkyard) that could feel unpolished. The product is "landed in heaven" clean, and "yard" can feel like dirt and gravel.

15. FRONT

The storefront. The front of the house. Front and center. "Hold down the front." Your business's front is what the world sees, but behind it, your team is running everything.

  • One syllable. Five letters.
  • "Open Front." "Check Front." "Front is running."
  • "Storefront" without the "store." What you show the world.
  • "Hold down the front" = manage your business, keep things running.
  • "Front" as military/strategic: the front line. Where the action is.
  • "Put up a front" = project confidence. Your AI team is your front. You look bigger than you are.

Trademark check: Front (front.com) is a customer communication platform. $300M+ raised. Major SaaS company. Same business-tools space. DEAD.

16. CAMP

Base camp. Summer camp. Boot camp. Camp is where you set up, where you train, where you prepare. It's temporary at first (a tent) and becomes permanent (a base).

  • One syllable. Four letters.
  • "Open Camp." "Check Camp." "What's running at Camp?"
  • "Set up Camp" = start your business. Plant your flag.
  • Summer camp energy: fun, productive, community. "The fun way to run your business."
  • Base camp energy: serious, strategic, the place you launch from.
  • Boot camp energy: get things done, level up, build strength.
  • A 16-year-old at Camp. A 55-year-old running Camp. Both feel right.

Trademark check: Basecamp (project management, $100B+ valuation). They don't own "Camp" alone but the association is strong. Camp (camp.com) is a kids' retail brand. Mixed territory.

Risk: Basecamp association is real but fading. "Camp" alone is different enough. The bigger risk: "camp" can sound temporary. You want permanence. Counter: every great base was once just a camp.

17. BENCH (revisited under different angle)

Already killed above for Bench Accounting. But the concept is strong enough to note: the workbench where you build things + the team bench where your players wait to go in. If the trademark conflict weren't there, this would be top 3.

Part 5: The Top 5

After filtering through every candidate against all of Patrik's criteria: lemonade stand energy, team energy, start from zero, 16 or 55, fun, universal, app-store clean, verb potential, "landed in heaven" compatible.

#5: SQUAD

The pitch: Your AI squad. Built from scratch. Ready to work.

Why it's here:

  • Generational crossover. "Squad" resonates with Gen Z (squad goals), millennials (squad up), and boomers (military squads). Everyone has a squad.
  • Gaming native. "Squad up" is a gaming call to action. The product IS a game.
  • "Build your Squad" is the product in three words.
  • One syllable. Sharp SQ opening (unusual, memorable). Hard D ending (decisive).
  • "Squad: The fun way to run your business." Natural tagline.
  • "I've got a Squad on it." Power statement.

Why it's #5:

  • It leans casual. "I run my enterprise through Squad" sounds a little informal for a CEO.
  • No inherent "place" quality. A squad is people, not a location. The product is also a place (rooms, worlds).
  • Can't become a verb easily. "Squad that" doesn't work.

Tagline pairings:

  • "Squad up."
  • "Build your Squad."
  • "Your Squad. Always on."

#4: LOT

The pitch: An empty lot. A blank canvas. Build whatever you want on it. Your lot in life, defined by you.

Why it's here:

  • The ultimate "start from zero" word. An empty lot is NOTHING. Then you build on it and it becomes everything. That IS the product journey.
  • Three letters. Shortest possible name. Instant to type, say, spell.
  • "Build on your Lot." "Check my Lot." "Open Lot."
  • "Your lot in life" = your destiny, your share, your portion. Deep philosophical resonance.
  • A lot is physical. You can stand on it. You can picture the empty dirt, then picture the building that goes up.
  • Construction vertical alignment: AOM targets construction companies. They know lots. They build on lots. The metaphor is native to the audience.
  • "A million lots, one platform." Clean.

Why it's #4:

  • Three letters might be TOO minimal for App Store presence and brand weight.
  • "Lot" as "a bunch of stuff" is a more common usage that could dilute the real-estate meaning.
  • Doesn't carry team energy. A lot is a place, but it doesn't imply people working.
  • "I run everything through Lot" sounds slightly odd. The object needs "my" in front of it: "my Lot."

Tagline pairings:

  • "Build on your Lot."
  • "Start with nothing. Build everything."
  • "Your Lot. Your rules."

#3: STOOP

The pitch: Where the neighborhood gathers. Where ideas start. Where business is born. Step outside, sit on the Stoop, and build.

Why it's here:

  • Nobody in tech sounds like this. The word is completely unexpected in an AI product context. "Why didn't I think of that" factor is high.
  • East Coast DNA connects to Patrik's background (DC, Silver Spring, Maryland). Stoop culture is real culture. It's where neighborhoods happen.
  • A stoop is democratic. No velvet rope. No credentials. Anyone can sit on the stoop.
  • "Stoop sale" = the urban lemonade stand. DIRECT connection to the energy Patrik wants.
  • One syllable. Five letters. Hard ST opening, warm OO middle, punchy P ending.
  • "Open Stoop." "Check my Stoop." "I'm on the Stoop." "Stoop sale" as a product feature name (marketplace).
  • It carries BOTH place energy (you sit there) and people energy (the neighborhood gathers there).
  • A 16-year-old on the stoop selling candy. A 55-year-old holding court on the stoop. Both are real images.
  • "Stoop: The fun way to run your business." Has personality.

Why it's #3:

  • Regional. Not everyone in America knows "stoop." In the Southwest, it's a "porch." In the Midwest, it's "the front step." International audiences might not get it at all.
  • Could sound too casual/small for enterprise ambitions. "I manage my operation from Stoop" is quirky, which could be a strength or a weakness.
  • The word has a secondary meaning: "to stoop" = to lower yourself. "Don't stoop to their level." Negative connotation there.

Tagline pairings:

  • "Sit down. Build up."
  • "Your Stoop. Your business."
  • "Where it all starts."

#2: CREW

The pitch: Your crew. The people who roll with you. Built from nothing. Loyal. Always working.

Why it's here:

This is the "The Team" energy perfected. "The Team" is clunky (the article, the generic word). "Crew" is the same feeling with half the syllables and twice the personality.

  • One syllable. Four letters. Clean.
  • "I've got a Crew" is the most natural sentence in the English language. It sounds like something Patrik would actually say.
  • Film crews. Construction crews. Flight crews. These are people who execute at the highest level.
  • "Build your Crew" = the product in three words. You start with nothing. You add agents. You build your crew.
  • Crew implies loyalty. A team is professional. A crew is personal. You chose these people. They chose you.
  • "Crew: The fun way to run your business." Tagline-ready.
  • A 16-year-old: "Check my Crew. I've got 3 agents running." Game energy.
  • A 55-year-old: "I manage everything through Crew." Confident and clear.
  • "A million crews, one platform." Direct.
  • The word works as identity: "I'm a Crew user" = "I'm part of something."
  • Construction vertical alignment: every contractor knows what a crew is. They RUN crews. The metaphor is their daily life.

Why it's #2 and not #1:

CrewAI exists. It's an open-source AI agent framework. It's in our space. Not the same product (developer framework vs consumer platform), and not the same audience (engineers vs SMBs), but it's in the conversation. Anyone Googling "Crew AI agents" will hit CrewAI results. You'd be sharing mindshare in the early days.

That said: Figma launched when Adobe was the only word in design. Notion launched when Evernote was the only word in notes. If the product is good enough, you define the word. CrewAI is a developer tool. Crew (without the AI) could own the consumer space.

Tagline pairings:

  • "Build your Crew."
  • "Your Crew. Always on."
  • "Roll with a Crew."
  • "Crew: The fun way to run your business."
  • "Every business needs a Crew."

#1: CORNER

The pitch: Your corner. Your corner store, your corner office, your corner of the world. Start on the corner, end up cornering the market.

Why it's the one:

  1. It carries the ENTIRE journey in one word. A kid selling lemonade on the corner. A business owner running the corner store. A CEO in the corner office. A company that corners the market. The word grows WITH you. It never stops fitting.

  2. It's the lemonade stand that grew up. Every neighborhood has a corner. Every kid has stood on one. The corner is where you set up shop with nothing and start selling. That IS "lemonade stand" energy, but it's not limited to lemonade. It's ANY business, at ANY scale, from ANY starting point.

  3. "Hold down your Corner" is the product pitch. Your agents hold down the corner for you. They're running your business while you're living your life. "I've got agents holding down my Corner." That sentence IS the product.

  4. Two syllables. Six letters. C-O-R-N-E-R. Hard C opening (memorable, same family as Kodak, Kova). Strong R ending (rolls off the tongue). Rhythmic. Satisfying to say. Not too short (won't get lost), not too long (easy to type and remember).

  5. It's a real, physical, visual thing. You can picture a corner. You can stand on one. You can point to one. It exists in the real world. Like Loft, it lives in your gut, not just your head. When Patrik said he loved Loft, he loved it because it was REAL. Corner is real.

  6. "Corner the market" is built into the DNA. No other name has a built-in phrase about business domination. "I started on a Corner. Now I corner the market." That's a whole brand campaign in one sentence.

  7. Street culture, business culture, design culture. All one word. The corner is where hip-hop was born (cyphers on the corner). It's where businesses are born (corner store). It's where architecture happens (corner lots are premium). Patrik's creative DNA (hip-hop, street culture, 90s edge) and business DNA (construction, SMBs, building something from nothing) converge in this word.

  8. "A million corners, one platform." Every business gets their own corner. Their corner of the world. Their corner of the market. The multi-tenant metaphor is built in: each client has a corner.

  9. Age-proof.

    • A 16-year-old: "I built my first business on Corner." Sounds like a game you'd download.
    • A 55-year-old: "My entire operation runs through Corner." Sounds like a tool a serious person uses.
    • Neither feels weird. Neither feels out of place.

  10. Verb potential. "Corner it." "I'll Corner that." "Cornered." When you assign a task to your AI team, you're cornering it. When your business locks down a market, you've cornered it. The verb IS the ambition.

  11. Trademark territory is open. No major AI/SaaS platform called Corner. No VC-backed consumer product. The word is common but unclaimed in this specific space. corner.app, getcorner.com, mycorner.com, usecorner.com are all reasonable domain paths.

  12. It matches "landed in heaven" without fighting it. A corner can be clean, bright, premium. Think of the corner unit in a luxury building: floor-to-ceiling windows, light from two sides, the best view. The "heaven" aesthetic isn't at odds with "corner." It elevates it. Your Corner isn't a street corner. It's THE corner. The best position in the building.

  13. Construction vertical native. Corner lots. Cornerstones. Corner units. The construction companies AOM targets understand "corner" instinctively. It's THEIR language.

  14. The "why didn't I think of that" factor. An AI platform where you build your business is called "Corner." Of course it is. You start on the corner. You corner the market. Your AI team holds down the corner. Every connection clicks in hindsight. That's the sign.

Bonus: The Naming System

If the product is Corner, every feature gets a street-level name:

Feature Street Name
Your dashboard Your Corner
Agent rooms The Block (your corner of the block)
Starting a new business Setting up on the Corner
Marketplace/templates The Strip (shops along the strip)
Team chat The Stoop (sit and talk)
Analytics The Ledger (from the corner store)
Onboarding Grand Opening

This isn't required. But it shows how deep the metaphor goes. It's not a surface-level name. It's a WORLD.

The Verdict

Corner.

Not invented. Not Italian. Not clever. Just real.

A kid on the corner selling lemonade. A business owner holding down their corner. A company that cornered the market.

Six letters. Two syllables. Your grandmother can say it. Your teenager thinks it's fire.

The word starts where you start (nothing, just a corner) and ends where you're going (cornering the market). The name IS the journey.

"I started on a Corner. Now I corner the market."

That's a Super Bowl ad. That's a billboard. That's a brand.

Runner-Up Ladder

  3. Lot (start from zero, empty lot to empire, construction native. Might feel too thin.)
  4. Squad (gaming native, generational crossover, "squad up." Might feel too casual.)
